Every other event scans the same unchanged tail, so deleting class-one events identifies the new first row with the old tail at every prefix and decreases the remaining class numbers by one.

items.target: Class order, formulas (18)–(20) and both displayed classifications
items.argument: Within one class, timestamps increase while replacement values strictly decrease. Its final P value is the last input value, its Q value is the first timestamp, and successive replacements emit exactly adjacent cross-pairs. The recorded original and bumped classes match the example.

items.target: Exercise 2: symmetric chain characterization of each class
items.argument: Maintain the first-row entries as the minimum possible endpoints of increasing subsequences of each length. At the first endpoint greater than p, the previous endpoint extends to p, whereas a longer chain would contradict minimality. All shorter minima remain unchanged. Induction proves both directions of the stated simultaneous q,p chain characterization, including singleton chains.

items.target: Theorem B: transformed first rows and the exact inverse bumped array
items.argument: The chain characterization preserves each class under coordinate swap. Inside it the order reverses, interchanging the first P/Q rows. Every emitted (q_next,p_previous) becomes exactly (p_previous,q_next); all values remain distinct, so these are valid mutually inverse bumped arrays after sorting timestamps.

items.target: Theorem B: full induction and the involution corollary
items.argument: For n>0 the bumped array has n minus the positive first-row length entries. Induction on n swaps both lower tableaux, completing the first-row argument without assuming row-count equality. Injectivity of Theorem A then gives pi=pi^-1 iff P=Q and a bijection between all tableaux and involutions, including n=0.

items.target: The upper-left corner is the minimum
items.argument: Every existing cell can be reached from (1,1) inside the Young diagram by right then downward moves, each strictly increasing. The sorting proposal that continues onto page 55 remains outside this item until Algorithm S is proved.

items.target: Algorithm S and exercise 10: complete hole invariant
items.argument: Ignore the active hole value. All other edges remain ordered, and both upper/left neighbors are below both lower/right candidates. Initialization is immediate. After either finite move, the filled cell has four valid edges and both new predecessor bounds follow from the original row/column inequalities.

items.target: Algorithm S: the skipped test after S4 and the infinity tie
items.argument: The comparison uses the special sentinel relation, so two infinity candidates select S5. S4 therefore always moves a finite key and can safely return directly to S3. S5 either moves a finite key or removes a genuine outer corner and reaches S2 outside the shape.

items.target: Algorithm S: termination, content preservation and exact per-deletion cost
items.argument: Every finite move increases r+s within a finite Young shape; the last comparison sees two infinities. Exactly the original minimum disappears and one corner is removed. For actual corner (i,j), exactly i+j−1 S3 steps occur. Empty input and singleton are explicit; the incorrect reported coordinate is the already proved C0005.

items.target: Sorting by repeated S and the claimed tree-based O(n log n) comparison
items.argument: The minimum lemma and S invariants inductively output sorted keys. Prior insertions correctly construct the tableau; tie-breaking handles duplicate input. A complete binary heap with upward repair on insertion and smaller-child downward repair on deletion proves the stated alternative bound in a direct-access comparison model.

items.target: Exercise 11: restoring one deletion requires the missing key
items.argument: Distinct singleton keys yield identical final arrays and (r,s), so that information alone is insufficient. If the deleted minimum is known, start at the actual corner (r−1,s), move the larger upper/left neighbor into the hole, and finish with the deleted key at (1,1). Reversing each forward move uniquely selects its predecessor by the untouched row/column inequality.

items.target: Exercise 12: the exact total S3 count for an arbitrary shape
items.argument: Each original cell is removed once as a corner. Summing its cost i+j−1 gives sum_i binom(n_i+i,2)−binom(m+1,3), independently of tableau filling, including empty and singleton shapes.

items.target: Exercise 12 and page 55: exact minimum and the Theta(n^(3/2)) sorting minimum
items.argument: There are k positive-grid cells of weight i+j−1=k. Taking all lowest-weight cells is feasible as a Young shape. For n=t(t+1)/2+r, the minimum is t(t+1)(2t+1)/6+(t+1)r=sqrt(8/9)n^(3/2)+O(n). The attaining shape has O(sqrt n) width/height, so all preceding insertions also cost O(n^(3/2)).

items.target: Exercise 12 answer: average cost under both natural uniform distributions
items.argument: For a uniform permutation, the increasing-subsequence union bound gives Pr(width≥k)≤n^k/(k!)² and exponential tails beyond 2e sqrt n; transpose both tableaux for the height distribution. For a uniform tableau, the involution recurrence yields sqrt n≤t_n/t_(n−1)≤sqrt n+1 and Pr(width=l)≤n^(l/2)/l!. Transposition again handles height. Both measures have mean Theta(n^(3/2)) and overwhelmingly bounded width/height of order sqrt n; no sharper limit constant is claimed.

items.target: Every displayed forward deletion state and the full dual-tableau example
items.argument: The note records all sixteen finite sliding paths and their actual vacated corners. The first and third active states match the intermediate figures, and the corner labels reproduce every cell of diagram (26).

items.target: Dual tableau shape and commutation with transpose
items.argument: Removing outer corners in increasing key order fills left/upper cells later and hence with larger keys, proving that the record is a dual tableau of the same shape. Finite candidate selection is symmetric under transpose; the final infinity tie changes only the reported cursor, not the removed cell. Thus d and full dualization commute with transpose.

items.argument: On diagram (26), deleting 16 moves 15,11,8,7 to corner (5,1); deleting 15 moves 14,13,12,10,2 to corner (1,6). This verifies exactly the shown two-step state, without treating it as a proof of general involutivity.

items.target: Theorem C and exercise 13: deletion of the minimum from the input word
items.argument: If 2 precedes 1, deleting 1 changes only the first-row minimum and removes the unique 2 from the bumped word; induction on that shorter word completes the lower rows. If 2 follows 1, reverse the word using the proved exercise-5 transpose identity and use commutation of d with transpose. Both cases avoid circular dependence on Theorem D.

items.target: Theorem D: all three order-reversal identities
items.argument: Exercise 5 first gives the transposed insertion component under reversed recording order; biword symmetry gives the other transposed shape. Induction removes the original minimum using Theorem C in normal order and the greatest-letter deletion lemma in dual order. The definition of full dualization then identifies the missing corner. Symmetry proves (a), and composing (a),(b) with transpose commutation proves (c).

items.target: Full dualization is an involution under the opposite order
items.argument: Apply Theorem D(c) twice, each time in the current order. Both order reversals and column reversals cancel, so uniqueness of the correspondence gives E_dual(E(P))=P. Every tableau occurs in a pair by Theorem A, proving full involutivity including the empty case.

items.target: The two admissible local relations and all swaps in the displayed example
items.argument: For x<y<z, the definition is exactly xzy↔zxy or yxz↔yzx. Among the six adjacent pairs of 1546837, exactly 1/5,4/6,8/3 have an allowed neighboring intermediate value.

items.target: Row lemma for xzy↔zxy, including finite and infinity cases
items.argument: Let a be the first old row entry above x and c the first above z. If a<z, the outputs are (a,c,v),(c,a,v) with a<v≤z<c. Otherwise a=c and the outputs are (a,d,z),(a,z,d), z<a<d. These are admissible triples when finite; omitting infinity outputs leaves identical shorter words. Output multisets and resulting sorted rows agree.

items.target: Row lemma for yxz↔yzx, including short rows
items.argument: The common first insertion bumps b. In the resulting row the first entries a>x and c>z satisfy a≤y<b<c when finite. Inserting x,z changes different positions and commutes in the row; output triples (b,a,c),(b,c,a) are admissible. Infinity omissions give identical shorter outputs.

items.target: Exercise 4(a): invariance in an arbitrary prefix tableau and following suffix
items.argument: The row lemmas produce the same first row and equal or admissibly related bumped triples. Induction on the original number of lower rows proves identical full results, with an explicit empty-row base. A common following suffix then starts from equal tableaux and stays equal.

items.target: Exercise 4(b): constructive equivalence to the bottom-to-top row word
items.argument: For an increasing row A b B with A<x<b<B, move x left across B by successive K2 relations, then b left across A by K1: A b B x~b A x B. Applying this at each bumped row proves W(T)x~W(I(T,x)). Induction gives w~W(P(w)), so all words with the same P are connected. Identical words use the reflexive zero-step convention; distinct words have a nonempty connecting sequence.

items.target: The explicit canonical-word transformation in answer 4(b)
items.argument: Apply the proved row factorization with successive carried values 8,9,10,13. The four resulting rows are 1358(12)(16),269(15),4(10)(14),11(13), with the old bottom 17 unchanged, giving exactly the printed two canonical words.

items.target: Exercise 5: reversal of the input word gives the transposed tableau
items.argument: Reversing each admissible relation exchanges K1 with K2. The reversed canonical row word is the column word of T transpose, read bottom-to-top in each column. Inserting a decreasing column moves only within that new column: each incoming value exceeds all old row entries. Induction on columns proves that this word inserts to T transpose; invariance transfers the result to every original word.

items.target: Deleting the greatest letter from the input removes only its corner cell
items.argument: Induct over input prefixes. Greatest M initially appends to row one. Subsequent insertion paths are unchanged until hitting its cell; without M they stop there, while with M they bump M once to the end of the next row. All other entries coincide. This proves the source step even when later inputs move M.

items.target: Theorem D: the transposed components before identifying dualization
items.argument: Input reversal gives the transposed insertion tableau by exercise 5. Apply the proved biword inverse symmetry to exchange the two order roles and obtain the transposed recording component under value-order reversal. This determines the unknown component shape without assuming a dualization formula.

items.target: Theorem D(b) and (a): complete induction and the identity (29)
items.argument: Remove the least original value a. Theorem C identifies d(P) in normal order; the greatest-letter lemma identifies Y without a in dual order. Induction gives E(d(P)) transpose. By definition E(P) puts a at the first vacated corner and otherwise equals E(d(P)); equal full shapes force equal a cells. This proves (b); biword symmetry gives (a).

items.target: Theorem D(c) and both concluding insertion identities
items.argument: Compose recording-order reversal and value-order reversal. The pair becomes (E(P transpose) transpose,E(Q)), equal to (E(P),E(Q)) by proved transpose commutation. Reversing the word alone gives P transpose; reversing both word and key order, with sentinels exchanged, gives E(P).

items.target: The tableau recurrence, zero extension and uniqueness
items.argument: The maximum occupies an outer corner. Removing it gives exactly the disjoint valid shapes lambda−e_i; adding it reverses the operation. Invalid shapes count zero, trailing zero rows do nothing, and the empty shape counts one. Decreasing size makes the recurrence uniquely determine the function.

items.target: Every summand and diagram in the (6,4,4,1) example
items.argument: The removable corners are (1,6),(3,4),(4,1). Removing (2,4) would produce the invalid shape (6,3,4,1), hence its summand is zero; the trailing zero of (6,4,4,0) is discarded. These are precisely the three diagrams in (33).

items.target: Vandermonde determinant (35), including its sign
items.argument: The determinant with descending exponent rows is alternating and divisible by every x_i−x_j. Equal degree makes the quotient constant. The coefficient of x_1^(m−1)x_2^(m−2)... is +1 in both determinant and product, proving the stated sign and the empty/single-variable cases.

items.target: Exercise 17: the full polynomial identity
items.argument: The sum is alternating and homogeneous of degree binom(m,2)+1. Dividing by the Vandermonde leaves a symmetric linear polynomial a sum x_i+b y. Setting y=0 gives a=1; differentiating there and using the monomial-wise Euler identity gives b=binom(m,2). The identity holds also when variables coincide.

items.target: Every rational differentiation step in answer 17
items.argument: Off the diagonals, the logarithmic derivative is sum_(j!=i)1/(x_i−x_j). Pairing the terms x_i/(x_i−x_j) and x_j/(x_j−x_i) gives one per pair. This proves the displayed coefficient; the polynomial identity extends to coincident variables.

items.target: Dimension formula (34): extended domain, zero rows and normalization
items.argument: For L_i=lambda_i+m−i weakly decreasing and total size n≥0, an invalid rise in lambda forces equal adjacent L and a zero Vandermonde. A negative final lambda uses the explicit Volume-1 convention 1/k!=0 for negative integers. Appending a zero shifts old L by one and adds zero; all extra factors cancel. The empty-shape normalization follows.

items.target: Dimension formula (34): the complete recurrence verification
items.argument: With positive last row, summing the candidate formula for lambda−e_i factors as (n−1)!/product L_j! times sum_i L_i Delta(L−e_i). Invalid corner removals vanish by equal adjacent shifted values. Exercise 17 at y=−1 turns the sum into (sum L_i−binom(m,2))Delta(L)=nDelta(L), proving the recurrence and hence the formula.

items.target: The squared-count identity and the index change in (36)
items.argument: The proved pair bijection gives n!=sum_lambda f(lambda)^2. Padding each shape with n rows and setting q_i=lambda_i+n−i bijects the shapes with strictly decreasing nonnegative q of sum n(n+1)/2; the inverse has lambda_i≥0 because q_i≥n−i.

items.target: The unrestricted sum in (36) and its exact normalization
items.argument: Substitution of the dimension formula makes the ordered q sum equal to 1/n!. Its summand is symmetric and zero on repeated q values, so dropping the order restrictions multiplies it by exactly n!, yielding one. Empty size gives the single empty term one.

items.target: All hook lengths and marked cells in Figure 5
items.argument: Use h_ij=lambda_i−j+lambda_prime_j−i+1 for shape (7,6,6,4,2,2) and column lengths (6,6,4,4,3,3,1). The note lists and verifies every displayed length, the six-cell shaded hook at (2,3), and the maximum lambda_1+m−1.

items.target: The exact missing-length set in every row
items.argument: In row i, the distinct hook lengths lie in 1,...,L_i. For k>i, cells with j≤lambda_k have hook length above L_i−L_k, and cells with j>lambda_k have length below it. Thus the m−i distinct differences are precisely the missing values by counting. This proves the general statement and every dotted exception in Figure 5, using the known correction to L_2.

items.target: The complete hook-product proof of Theorem H
items.argument: The missing-length identity gives row product L_i!/product_(k>i)(L_i−L_k); multiplying gives product L_i!/Delta(L). Substitution into the already proved dimension formula yields n! divided by all hook lengths. Empty products and trailing zero rows are treated explicitly.

items.target: Validity of each hook probability and failure of independence
items.argument: A given hook cell is its minimum with probability 1/h, and all such events together exactly encode the tableau inequalities. In shape (2,2), events a=min(a,b,c) and b<d have probabilities 1/3 and 1/2 but joint probability 3/24=1/8, disproving independence while leaving the independently proved hook formula intact.

items.target: Row-bumping comparison for two consecutive distinct inputs
items.argument: If x<y, the second path is strictly right of the first in every common row and carries a larger next value; it ends no lower and in a strictly larger column. If x>y, its positions are weakly left and next carries are smaller; it must continue below the first endpoint and ends weakly left. The two cases prove both directions needed for standardization.

items.target: Repeated-label correspondence: forward construction with both labels repeated
items.argument: Lexicographically sort a multiset of (q,p) pairs and distinguish equal labels by occurrence order. Ordinary insertion gives a pair of tableaux. Within equal q blocks the standardized p inputs increase, so the new recording corners have distinct increasing columns. Apply biword inverse symmetry to prove the same property for equal p in the other tableau. Erasing occurrence tags yields weak rows and strict columns in both.

items.target: Repeated-label correspondence: full inverse and specialization
items.argument: Standardize each equal-value set of a semistandard pair from left to right by column. The ordinary inverse gives a biword. The converse row-bumping lemma makes p increase within every equal-q block; applying inverse symmetry also makes each p tag agree with occurrence order. Thus the recovered pairs are lexicographically sorted and restandardize to the original biword. Both directions invert, including empty input; distinct q gives the one-sided multiset case.

items.target: Ordered binary trees and balanced stack-operation words
items.argument: Encode a nonempty binary tree as S D(left) X D(right). The first return to zero uniquely decomposes every balanced prefix-nonnegative word into this form, proving an inverse recursion and preserving node count, including the empty case.

items.target: Stack-generated permutations and the corrected forbidden 312 pattern
items.argument: A desired output forces pushing unread entries through it or popping it if already on top; a buried value is impossible. A 312 pattern forces a larger still-pending key above the needed smaller one. Conversely, any greedy failure gives exactly such a pattern from the earlier output that forced the blocking key onto the stack. Thus stack words, their outputs and the corrected avoidance class are in bijection.

items.target: The two-row tableau/ballot correspondence and example (37)
items.argument: Put S positions in the first row and X positions in the second. Column inequalities s_j<x_j are exactly the nonnegative prefix-balance condition, proving both directions. The displayed word gives rows (1,2,3,6,7,10) and (4,5,8,9,11,12).

items.target: Catalan and general ballot counts, with both boundary conventions
items.argument: The two-row rectangular hook product is (n+1)!n!, giving (2n)!/((n+1)!n!). For shape (n,m), the dimension formula gives (n+m)!(n−m+1)/((n+1)!m!). Removing an initial S gives the strict-prefix formula for nonempty words with n>m; the empty word is handled separately.

items.target: The full rectangle-splitting bijection and every displayed intermediate array
items.argument: Entries ≤n form a two-row ideal (a,b) with a+b=n. Its complement, rotated 180 degrees and relabeled x→2n+1−x, has the same shape. Conversely, the two tableaux fill complementary regions and every crossing edge goes from a value≤n to one>n, proving validity and uniqueness. The explicit split and rotated arrays in (38) are reproduced.

items.target: Exercise 7: both increasing and decreasing subsequence lengths
items.argument: Reuse the minimum-endpoint invariant for the first-row length. Increasing subsequences of the reversed word correspond exactly to decreasing subsequences of the original. The proved reversal/transposition identity therefore turns width into height, proving the second half with the same domain.

items.target: The Catalan count for permutations avoiding a decreasing triple
items.argument: By exercise 7, absence of a 321 subsequence is exactly insertion-tableau height at most two. The pair correspondence and the rectangle-splitting bijection identify these permutations with all tableaux of shape (n,n), hence with the Catalan count and binary trees.

items.target: Diagram (39), tableau labels and general acyclic graphs
items.argument: The graph has precisely the row/column neighbor edges of shape (6,4,4,1). Increasing labels along edges are exactly tableau inequalities. In any finite DAG, increasing distinct labels are equivalent to topological vertex order; a vertex with no predecessor exists, giving an inductive construction.

items.target: A general poset count need not divide n!
items.argument: The four-element poset a<c, b<c, b<d has two extensions starting with a and three starting with b, hence five in total. Since 5 does not divide 24, a universal integer hook-product divisor formula is impossible; no broader impossibility claim about formulas or algorithms is inferred.

items.target: Exercise 16: the exact count 80080
items.argument: The hook rows are (9,7,6,5,2,1),(6,4,3,2),(5,3,2,1),(1). Their product is 2^7 3^6 5^2 7, while 15! is 2^11 3^6 5^3 7^2 11 13. Their quotient is 2^4·5·7·11·13=80080, with no enumeration.

items.target: The involution recurrence and all eleven tabulated values
items.argument: Reuse the fixed-point/partner decomposition from P0414 with t_0=t_1=1. The note supplies each recurrence addition through t_10, verifying 1,1,2,4,10,26,76,232,764,2620,9496.

items.target: The exact number of involutions with k transpositions
items.argument: Choose the 2k nonfixed elements, order them into k distinguished pairs, divide by 2^k for pair reversals and by k! for pair order. This gives n!/((n−2k)!2^k k!) for every permitted k, including the empty term, and summing gives (41).

items.target: The Hermite-polynomial expression and its exact normalization
items.argument: The official DLMF generating function exp(2xz−z²) defines H_n. Coefficient extraction gives its finite polynomial sum, valid also for complex x. Substituting x=−i/sqrt(2) and multiplying by i^n2^(−n/2) makes each phase equal to one and each power of two equal to 2^(−k), exactly recovering the involution sum.

items.target: Exercise 25: the involution exponential generating function
items.argument: Write r=n−2k in the exact cycle-count sum. The double sum factors into sum z^r/r! times sum z^(2k)/(2^k k!), giving exp(z+z²/2). Each formal coefficient has finitely many terms, so no analytic interchange assumption is needed.

items.target: The full cycle-length generalization in answer 25
items.argument: For c_s cycles of each allowed positive length, divide n! by product s^(c_s)c_s! for rotations and equal-length cycle ordering. Summing independently gives exp(sum_(s in S) z^s/s), including finite cutoffs, the involution case and empty S. Infinite S is valid coefficientwise because only lengths≤n can contribute.

items.target: Exact consecutive-term ratio, unimodality and the shifted central lattice
items.argument: Cancel factorials in (43). With r=n−2k the ratio is at least 1 exactly when r²≥n+2; the mode is within O(1) of (n−sqrt(n))/2. Define actual alpha and beta using ceiling and floor, allowing any fractional lattice shift.

items.target: Every constant and the uniform remainder in the corrected Stirling expansion (46)
items.argument: The note reduces all three log-factorials to two Taylor series and records the cancellations. With u=n^-1/4 and z=ux, the remainder is O(u³(1+|z|⁵)) uniformly for |z|≤n^epsilon. The missing n is an existing 1999 correction.

items.target: The discarded discrete terms and bound (47)
items.argument: Unimodality reduces each tail to its first omitted term at x=±n^(1/4+epsilon)+O(1). The uniform expansion bounds it by exp(C_n−2n^(2epsilon)+O(n^(3epsilon−1/4))). There are at most n terms, so the tails are negligible relative to every algebraic correction.

items.target: Factor (48), every quadratic exponential term and corrected (49)
items.argument: After taking out exp(C_n+u²/3), expand exp(uA+u²B+r) with A=2z−4z³/3 and B=−4z⁴/3. The u² polynomial is 2z²−4z⁴+8z⁶/9 and the uniform weighted remainder is O(u³(1+|z|⁹)). The coefficient 8/9 is the existing 1999 correction.

items.target: Translated Euler summation (50), boundary signs and the remainder constant
items.argument: Integrate the periodic B1 times f prime over unit intervals on alpha+Z, then integrate by parts repeatedly. The periodic Bernoulli Fourier coefficients bound the remainder by 4/(2pi)^r times the L1 norm of f^(r), including r=1 by the direct B1 bound.

items.target: Derivative scaling and integrability in (51)
items.argument: Apply the chain rule to f(x)=n^(t/4) g(n^-1/4 x). Differentiation preserves the form polynomial times exp(−2y²), so the absolute derivative integral is finite and R_r=O(n^((t+1−r)/4)) uniformly in the lattice shift.

items.target: Original endpoint-extension estimate and the defective 2006 replacement
items.argument: Fixed polynomial factors multiply exp(−2n^(2epsilon)); this proves the original O(exp(−2n^epsilon)) and a sufficient O(exp(−n^(2epsilon))). For t=0 the actual unnormalized integral tail is asymptotic to 1/2 n^(1/4−epsilon) exp(−2n^(2epsilon)), refuting only the stronger replacement in the errata.

items.target: Equation (52) with every fixed algebraic precision and an arbitrary lattice shift
items.argument: For prescribed K choose Euler order r≥t+1+4K. All boundary and integral-tail terms are superpolynomially small using the valid bound, and the remainder is O(n^-K). Odd t need not cancel exactly on the shifted finite grid, but its residual has this same bound.

items.target: Exercise 26: the half-line gamma integral including t=0
items.argument: Substitute v=2x²/sqrt(n) to obtain n^((t+1)/4) Gamma((t+1)/2)/2^((t+3)/2). The integral converges at both ends for every nonnegative integer t and n>0.

items.target: Exercise 26: parity and the full-line factorial formula
items.argument: Odd integrands integrate to zero. For t=2j use Gamma(j+1/2)=(2j)!sqrt(pi)/(4^j j!), with the base Gaussian integral established by squaring and polar coordinates. This gives exactly n^((t+1)/4)sqrt(pi)t!/[2^((3t+1)/2)(t/2)!].

items.target: The sum following (52), coefficient −1/24 and removal of the epsilon loss
items.argument: The normalized Gaussian moments are 1/4,3/16,15/64, giving 2mu2−4mu4+(8/9)mu6=−1/24. Bound the polynomial remainder using |z|⁹≤1+z^10 and the already established Gaussian summation, yielding absolute O(u²) without a 9epsilon loss.

items.target: All factors and the 7/24 correction in (53)
items.argument: Multiply the normalized sum by exp(C_n+u²/3); the main factors give n^(n/2)exp(−n/2+sqrt(n)−1/4)/sqrt(2), and 1/3−1/24=7/24. The relative remainder is O(n^-3/4), and the discrete tails are smaller than every retained order.

items.target: Extension to any fixed asymptotic order
items.argument: Retain more Stirling and Taylor terms; each omitted part is bounded by an arbitrarily high u power times a fixed polynomial in z, integrable with the Gaussian weight. Increase the Euler order as needed. Under (u,z)→(−u,−z) the exact expressions are invariant, so odd powers have odd coefficient polynomials and vanish on integration.

items.argument: Each restart follows the successive minima of the unused sequence, hence exactly one insertion class. Previously skipped entries cannot become eligible to its left after p decreases. The outputs are infinity followed by prior class members, exactly the bump outputs. Every step fills one slot; the finite line length strictly decreases between rows.

items.target: Exercise6: why odd classes count the fixed points
items.argument: Transposition preserves both the involution pair set and its chain-length class. A class with first coordinates a1<…<ah must therefore have pairs (aj,a_(h+1−j)); it has exactly one diagonal pair when h is odd and none otherwise.

items.target: Exercise6: the bumped array is an involution with s−k fixed points
items.argument: A class on a1,…,ah bumps pairs (a_(j+1),a_(h+1−j)), j<h, a reverse involution on a2,…,ah. It has a fixed point exactly when h is even. Disjoint class label sets give a genuine smaller involution on their union, with s−k fixed points.

items.target: Exercise6: induction and the parity of missing lower columns
items.argument: Apply induction to the n−s bumped keys on their ordered label subset. The lower tableau has s−k odd columns.
